Operating format

A working room for leaders who own the AI decision.

This is not a passive webinar. The session is designed to surface what leaders are actually seeing, where decisions are stuck, and which operating questions deserve deeper summit work.

Stage 01

Executive Framing Keynote

A concise opening view of national AI adoption momentum, business pressure, and the leadership questions executives need to settle.

Stage 02

Readiness Diagnostic Discussion

Moderated prompts let each executive compare adoption posture, governance maturity, measurement gaps, and risk tolerance.

Stage 03

Summit Cohort Invitation Path

Qualified participants can be routed into the fall series, member nominations, executive research briefs, and 2027 summit planning.

The room

Small enough for candor. Senior enough to matter.

The point is not to agree on a slogan about AI. The point is to compare where leadership teams are moving, where they are hesitating, who has real ownership, and how trust is being earned with employees, customers, boards, and regulators.

Audience
Executives and senior operators accountable for AI strategy, business value, risk, technology, data, or workforce adoption.
Access
Invitation-only, capped at nine executive participants for a moderated exchange rather than broadcast attendance.
Outcome
A clearer readiness baseline and a path into the MOJO AI Summits cohort for deeper peer work.

Moderated prompts

The questions every AI leadership team is already carrying.

The discussion is built around eight live questions. Each one is designed to expose operating reality, not produce generic optimism.

01

Are we still advancing AI adoption?

Are organizations moving forward, stalled, or regressing nationally, and what forces explain the change?

02

Are we moving away from frontier models?

If teams are shifting toward smaller, specialized, open, private, or embedded models, how fast is it happening and at what risk?

03

How do we measure AI value?

What counts as output, outcome, ROI, and business value, and how do leaders know whether AI work is being done right?

04

Where does AI sit in the organization?

Who is using it today, who should be using it, who should not be using it, and who owns the operating model?

05

Whose hands have been on your AI?

When tools produce an output, who touched it, reviewed it, authorized it, and do customers know or care?

06

Human in the loop, yes or no?

Where does human review create trust, where does it create friction, and how should leaders extrapolate that line?

07

How do we work with people who fear AI?

What drives resistance or detestation, and how should leaders respond without dismissing legitimate concerns?

08

Are regulations helping yet?

Are AI rules driving governance, protection, or privacy effectively, when will they, and who will make that happen?
